subject: system-design
title: Domain Name System (DNS)
summary: How the internet turns a human-friendly name into a machine address, using a hierarchical, heavily cached lookup that doubles as a load-balancing layer.

blocks.text: Computers route traffic by IP address, but people remember names. DNS is the phone book of the internet: it maps a human-friendly name like example.com to the IP address a client actually connects to. Every request to a website starts with this lookup.
DNS isn't one server; it's a tree of authority. A lookup walks down the hierarchy until it finds the server that holds the answer.

items: Root servers sit at the top of the tree and point to the right TLD servers.
TLD servers form one tier per top-level domain (.com, .org, .net) and point to the authoritative server.
Authoritative servers are the source of truth for a specific domain and hold its actual records.

blocks.text: A client usually asks a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP, to do all the work and return a final answer. The resolver then does the iterative part: it queries the root, then the TLD, then the authoritative server in turn, following each referral until it has the IP. The client sees one question and one answer; the chasing happens behind the resolver.
Caching and TTL at every layer

Walking the whole hierarchy for every request would be slow, so answers are cached everywhere: in the browser, the operating system, and the resolver. Each record carries a TTL (time to live) that says how long it may be cached before it must be looked up again. Short TTLs make changes propagate faster; long TTLs cut latency and load.

DNS does more than map names. It's a first, coarse layer of traffic steering. A name can resolve to several IPs, and the response can vary by who's asking, which spreads users across servers and regions.

items: Multiple A records let the resolver hand out different IPs to spread load.
Geo or latency routing returns the address of the nearest or fastest data center.
Failover drops an unhealthy address so new lookups avoid a downed site.

blocks.title: The cold-lookup cost
blocks.text: A cache miss can mean several round trips up the hierarchy before the first byte of your page even loads. That latency is exactly why caching and TTLs matter so much.
DNS is itself a globally distributed, cached, hierarchical system. It is a working example of the same patterns you'll apply to your own designs.
